analysis.one_liner: Hands a copper mining company federal land at Oak Flat, Arizona, in exchange for private conservation parcels.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Oak Flat land swap 235-186 in October 2011, but the Senate held only a hearing and never voted before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have handed a copper mining company full title to about 2,422 acres of federal land at Oak Flat, Arizona, in exchange for about 5,300 acres of the company's private land that would be added to national forests and conservation areas. The company would get guaranteed exploration permits, a one-year deadline to complete the swap, and treatment of the land like any private mining site. The House passed it 235-186 in October 2011, but the Senate never voted and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Resolution Copper Mining, LLC — a copper mining venture backed by two of the world's largest mining companies — would receive full title to federal land at Oak Flat, usable for mining under the same rules as any private owner, plus guaranteed special-use permits for exploration and a one-year congressional instruction to complete the exchange. The town of Superior, Arizona, could buy about 545 acres of federal land at appraised value, and the bill's findings cite jobs in a high-unemployment former mining region.

how_it_helps.text: Transfers full title to approximately 2,422 acres of federal land in Pinal County to Resolution Copper, available for mining and related activities under the laws governing private land.

Requires the Secretary of Agriculture, on the company's request, to issue special use permits for mineral exploration under and within the Oak Flat Withdrawal Area within 30 and 90 days respectively, overriding the area's existing withdrawal from mining.

Requires values to be equal or equalized and lets the Secretary accept a cash equalization payment of up to 25 percent of the total value, while barring any federal payment back to the company if its land is worth more.
Directs the town of Superior, Arizona, to receive about 545 acres of federal land (cemetery and airport parcels) at fair market value for local development.

Adds roughly 4,300 acres of the company's private land to the San Pedro Riparian and Las Cienegas National Conservation Areas, the national forests, and BLM management, securing habitat and riparian protection for those parcels.

Requires Resolution Copper to surrender without compensation its rights to commercially extract minerals under Apache Leap, withdraws Apache Leap from mining and mineral leasing, and requires a management plan to protect its natural and cultural resources.
The bill's findings frame the exchange as creating jobs in a high-unemployment former mining region and supplying a 'world-class' domestic copper deposit.

analysis.who_pays: The public: the United States gives up roughly 2,422 acres of federal land at Oak Flat in Pinal County, Arizona, including the Oak Flat Campground's about 50 acres of public campsites, and loses the ability to keep the surface out of mine operations. Affected Indian tribes, for whom the area is a culturally significant site and whom the bill requires the government to consult, stand to lose access and the character of the place. Taxpayers also bear the risk that the appraisal methods in the bill value the land below what the copper under it is worth.

drawbacks.text: The exchange is written for a single named company: it conveys title to federal land including the Oak Flat Campground, requires government-to-government consultation with affected Indian tribes but does not condition the transfer on their consent, and terminates the Oak Flat withdrawal that had kept the area off-limits to mining.

The required appraisal must include an income capitalization analysis 'which may be utilized' to set the land's value, and no reappraisal is required for at least three years — a method critics can use to value land by its current income rather than the copper beneath it, capping what the company must pay or convey to equalize.

The environmental review must be completed within three years of the mine plan and would then be 'the basis for all decisions' on every federal authorization for the mine and its power, water, tailings, and waste facilities, compressing review of one of the largest proposed mines in the country into a fixed deadline.

The bill bars imposing restrictions on the company's mining beyond those that apply to ordinary privately owned land near Apache Leap, and shields its existing unpatented mining claims from any impairment.

The value adjustment payment is owed only if actual production exceeds the quantity assumed in the appraisal analysis, so if the deposit yields as much or less than projected, the public receives nothing beyond the exchanged parcels.

Block-cave mining of the kind proposed for this deposit is known to cause surface subsidence, meaning the conveyed surface land could physically collapse over the ore body — a cost borne by the land once it is no longer public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public side of the trade is real: roughly 4,300 acres added to conservation areas and national forests, protection for Apache Leap, and a development opportunity for Superior, Arizona. But the heart of the bill is a conveyance of federal land over a major copper deposit to one named company, with appraisal methods and a three-year environmental review deadline structured to speed the transfer and limit what the company owes. The company surrenders Apache Leap mineral rights and pays exchange costs, yet keeps full mining rights on the conveyed land with restrictions capped at private-land levels. On balance the bill's design serves the mining venture far more than the public.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 235-186 in October 2011, but the Senate committee held only one hearing and the Congress ended with no Senate vote.

narrative.text: Representative Paul Gosar introduced the bill on May 13, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
The committee ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 26-19 on July 13, 2011, and formally reported it with H. Rept. 112-246 on October 14, 2011.
Floor amendments by Representatives Lujan, Markey, and Grijalva were rejected, and a motion to recommit with instructions to bar exchanges with companies doing business with Iran failed 187-237.
The House passed the bill 235-186 on October 26, 2011, with 228 of 241 Republicans voting yes and only 7 of 192 Democrats joining them.

The Senate received the bill on October 31, 2011, referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and held a hearing on February 9, 2012, but the committee never reported it and the full Senate never voted before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oak Flat stayed in public hands, so the affected tribes, campground users, and conservation advocates kept the land and the mine had no federal title or guaranteed permits. Resolution Copper received nothing in this Congress and would have to start over with a new bill.

for.what_they_did: Reported the rule that structured floor debate, waived points of order against the committee substitute, and limited amendments

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost entirely by party: 228 of 241 Republicans voted yes while only 7 of 192 Democrats joined them, and all 187 yes votes on the motion to recommit were Democrats.

industries.industry: Copper mining (Resolution Copper, a venture of Rio Tinto and BHP)
industries.note: The bill conveys title to federal land sitting over one of the nation's largest undeveloped copper deposits to a single named company, guarantees its exploration permits, and limits future restrictions to those applying to ordinary private land — the bill even defines the company and its affiliates by name.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and public lands users
industries.note: Oak Flat, including a developed 50-acre campground, would leave public ownership, while the conservation parcels the company conveys in return are scattered acreage elsewhere in Arizona — a net loss of access at the site that matters most.
